questions.q: When is the value of this inside a normal (non-arrow) function decided?
questions.explain: this behaves like a hidden parameter filled in by the call site. The same function gets different values from different calls.
options: When the function is first attached to an object
Each time the function is called, from the way it is called

questions.q: What is this inside whoAmI for the call shop.branch.whoAmI()?
questions.explain: Only the object directly before the method name counts: the value before the last dot (or bracket).

questions.q: In an ES module, a function that uses this is called as fn(), with no dot. What is this?
questions.explain: ES modules are strict mode, and a plain call in strict mode gets this = undefined. Reading a property of it throws, so the mistake shows up at once.

questions.q: In an old, non-strict script, a function called as count() runs this.total = (this.total || 0) + 1. What happens?
questions.explain: In sloppy mode a plain call gets this = globalThis, so the function writes to the global object. Every other script can see and break that value. Strict mode throws instead.
options: It silently creates and updates a global variable called total
It updates a property on the function

questions.q: Which code runs in sloppy mode?
questions.explain: Modules and classes are always strict; the directive makes anything strict. CommonJS files and classic browser scripts are sloppy unless they opt in.
options: A file loaded as an ES module
A function whose body starts with "use strict"
A CommonJS file with no "use strict" line

questions.q: const { add } = basket; add("RICE-5"); throws Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'items'). Why?
questions.explain: const { add } = basket is the same as const add = basket.add. The object is not carried along; only a call with a dot would supply it.
options: Destructuring makes a deep copy of the method
Destructuring copies only the function into a variable; calling add(...) is a plain call, so this is undefined

questions.q: What does the second argument in ["SALT"].map(basket.add, basket) do?
questions.explain: map, filter, forEach, find, some and every take an optional thisArg. It works, but a wrapper arrow (sku) => basket.add(sku) is clearer to most readers.
options: It is the starting value, like in reduce
It is the thisArg: map calls the callback with this set to basket

questions.q: What is the difference between fn.call(obj, a, b) and fn.apply(obj, [a, b])?
questions.explain: Both call now with an explicit this. Since spread exists, fn.call(obj, ...args) covers what apply was used for.
options: call returns a new function, apply calls now
Only how the arguments are passed: a list for call, one array for apply; both call fn immediately with this = obj

questions.q: What does const later = report.print.bind(report) do?
questions.explain: bind never calls anything and never changes the original function. It creates a bound function, which you can pass around safely.
options: Calls report.print now and stores the result
Returns a new function that, whenever it is called, calls report.print with this = report
Changes report.print so it is bound everywhere

questions.q: const bound = fn.bind(ada). Which call can make bound run fn with this = chidi?
questions.explain: Binding is permanent. The only call form that overrides it is new, which creates a fresh object and is not what any of these do.
options: None of them: a bound function always uses ada

questions.q: A constructor function is bound: const B = Account.bind(bank). What is this inside Account during new B("Ada")?
questions.explain: new is stronger than bind. The constructor fills in the new object, and bank is not touched. (Bound arrow functions still cannot be constructed, because arrows never can.)
options: A brand new object; the binding is ignored by new
It throws: bound functions cannot be constructed

questions.q: Where does an arrow function get its this?
questions.explain: Arrows have no this of their own. They look it up lexically, exactly as closures find outer variables. That is why arrows make good callbacks inside methods.
options: From the object before the dot when it is called
From the surrounding code where the arrow was written, like any outer variable

questions.q: An object literal in a module has total: () => this.items.length. What happens when you call cart.total()?
questions.explain: An object literal does not create a this; only functions do. The arrow uses the module's this. Write methods with method syntax: total() { … }.
options: It returns the number of items
It throws: the arrow's this comes from the module, where it is undefined
It returns undefined because arrows cannot return values
It returns the length of the global items array

questions.q: What does arrowFn.call(report) do to this inside the arrow?
questions.explain: Explicit binding only works on functions that have their own this. The arrow keeps using the this of the code around it.
options: Nothing: the arrow ignores the this it is called with; call still passes the other arguments

questions.q: Older code often has const self = this; at the start of a method, then uses self inside function callbacks. Why?
questions.explain: Before arrow functions, a variable was the only way to carry the method's this into a nested function. An arrow callback does this automatically.
options: To make a copy of the object
A function callback gets its own this from its caller, so the method saved its this in a normal variable that the callback can reach through its closure
self is a special keyword that means the current object
To make the method run in strict mode

questions.q: A class declares handle = (event) => this.process(event); as a class field. What is true?
questions.explain: Field initialisers run for each new instance, with this being that instance. Detaching obj.handle is safe, at the cost of one function per instance.
options: The arrow is stored once on the prototype and shared by all instances
Every instance gets its own arrow function, bound to that instance, stored as an own property
The arrow's this is the class itself

questions.q: A parent class has refund = () => "refunded" as an arrow field. A child class tries super.refund() in its own refund field. What happens?
questions.explain: super.method reads from the parent's prototype. An arrow field is an own property of each instance, and the child's field overwrites it on the same instance.
options: It calls the parent's arrow normally
super.refund is undefined: super looks on the parent's prototype, and arrow fields are not on any prototype
It calls the child's refund again, forever
It works only if the parent's field is static

questions.q: A function click listener is registered on a <ul> and handles clicks on the buttons inside it (event delegation). A button is clicked. What is this?
questions.explain: The browser calls a function listener with the element it is attached to. The clicked element is event.target. Reading those two properties is clearer than this.
options: The <ul>, the element the listener is registered on (the same as event.currentTarget)

questions.q: In Node.js, orders.on("paid", function (id) { … }) registers a listener on an EventEmitter. What is this when it runs?
questions.explain: EventEmitter calls function listeners with the emitter as this. An arrow listener keeps the surrounding this instead. To call your own method, register a wrapper.

questions.q: Why does bindAll read each prototype property with Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor instead of proto[name]?
questions.explain: Accessors run code when read. Inspecting the descriptor finds real methods without triggering getters, and leaves getters in place.
options: Reading proto[name] would run any getter with the prototype as this, which can throw or give nonsense; the descriptor shows whether there is a plain function value
proto[name] does not work for class prototypes
To skip methods that are enumerable

questions.q: What is this inside notifier.remind when you write setTimeout(notifier.remind, 1000)?
questions.explain: The expression notifier.remind only reads the function; the call happens later, inside the timer. Pass () => notifier.remind() or a bound function instead.
options: Not notifier: the timer calls the function itself (Node.js passes its timer object, browsers pass window)

questions.q: You need to pass mailer.send as a callback in one place. Which fix is the simplest and costs nothing elsewhere?
questions.explain: A wrapper arrow puts the dot back exactly where it is needed and leaves the class and its prototype untouched. Binding helpers pay off when many methods are handed out in many places.
options: Convert every method of the Mailer class to an arrow field
Pass a wrapper at the call site: (message) => mailer.send(message)
Switch the file to sloppy mode

questions.q: What is this at the top level of a file, outside every function?
questions.explain: ES modules are strict and have no top-level this. CommonJS wraps each file in a function called with this set to module.exports.
options: undefined in an ES module; module.exports in a CommonJS file
The file name as a string
The first function in the file

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Both objects hold the same function, but each call gets the object before its dot. Where the function was first written does not matter.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: whose() is a plain call in a module (strict mode), so this is undefined.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: call takes the arguments one by one; apply takes them as one array and spreads them into the parameters.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: bind fixed this and the first argument (2 percent). The next argument becomes amount; the extra 99 is ignored. The bound function expects one parameter fewer.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first bind is permanent. Binding the bound function again, or calling it with call, cannot change the this it passes to name.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The arrow uses the method's this, which is report. The function callback gets its own this from map's plain call: undefined (and ?. avoids the crash).
options:
Lagos-A Lagos-B
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The arrow was written at the top level of the module, where this is undefined; calling it as cart.countArrow() does not change that. The method gets cart from the dot.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The getter lives on the prototype, but this is the object the property was read on, ada. That is how one getter serves every object that inherits it.
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The second argument of map is used as this for each callback call, so this.percent is 7.5.
options: TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'percent')

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: pay lives once on the prototype. The arrow field is created for each instance as an own, enumerable property, so each till has its own refund.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: new overrides the binding: Account ran with a fresh object, which is an instance of Account. bank was never touched.
options: TypeError: BoundAccount is not a constructor

questions.q: The Function constructor always creates a sloppy-mode function. What does this print?
questions.explain: Strict mode passes the primitive as it is. Sloppy mode wraps a primitive in an object and replaces undefined with the global object, so both sloppy calls see an object.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A bound function's name is "bound " plus the original name, and its length is the original's minus any fixed arguments (none here).

questions.q: The runner loses this. Change only the last line so both jobs are charged by payments.
questions.explain: The wrapper arrow calls payments.charge(job) with a dot, so this is payments. payments.charge.bind(payments) works too.

questions.q: In the constructor, bind remind to the instance, so the detached remind works.
questions.explain: this.remind.bind(this) reads the prototype method and stores a bound copy as an own property with the same name. Destructuring then copies the bound function.

questions.q: Use call to run receipt.total on oldOrder, which has lines but no methods. Do not add anything to oldOrder.
questions.explain: call runs the borrowed method once with the this you choose. The receipt's method and data are unchanged.

questions.q: Write myBind(fn, thisValue, ...fixedArgs) without using bind: it returns a function that calls fn with thisValue, the fixed arguments and then the new ones. Calling the result with call must not change this.
questions.explain: A closure remembers fn, thisValue and fixedArgs; apply calls with the chosen this. Returning an arrow means the call-site this is ignored, just like a real bound function.

questions.q: priceList crashes because its callback is a function. Rewrite the callback so it uses the method's this.
questions.explain: An arrow has no this of its own, so inside it this is the priceList method's this: shop.

questions.q: Use bind (with null as this, since the function does not use it) to create addVat, which always uses a 7.5 percent rate.
questions.explain: bind can fix leading arguments as well as this. addVat passes 7.5 as ratePercent, then its own argument as kobo.

questions.q: Turn increment into an arrow function class field so that forEach(counter.increment) works.
questions.explain: The field is created for each instance, and the arrow takes this from that setup, which is the new instance. It stays bound however it is called.

questions.q: Write bindMethods(obj, names) that replaces each named method on obj with a copy bound to obj, and returns obj.
questions.explain: Each method is replaced by a bound version, so destructuring copies functions that no longer depend on the call site.
